case_study_insert.main_stem: Voltway Charging (VWC) is a private limited company in the electric-vehicle charging and energy retail sector, employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2018 by Sofia Alvarez, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. VWC plans to invest $720,000 in a rapid-charging hub network with solar canopies, financed by a $450,000 five-year bank loan and a $270,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $252,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.20 a unit and a selling price of $15.60, and produces 60,000 units a year. VWC faces a charger fault rate of 6.4% and rising billing complaints from fleet drivers. Sofia Alvarez consults her technicians before changing prices.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: VWC delivered 60,000 charging sessions last year, up 14% on the previous year, but 6.4% of sessions ended in a charger fault and 29 billing complaints were logged last month. Charger availability was 94.2%, against a 98% target, and the average session lasted 27 minutes. A survey of 280 fleet managers found 73% would pay $0.45 more per session for guaranteed charger availability, and 61% choose networks by reliability. Ten of the 32 technicians need high-voltage certification at $1,250 each.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Voltway Charging (VWC) for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate has risen from 4.9% to 5.65%, raising borrowing costs for variable-rate business loans. (2) Wholesale electricity prices have risen 15.2% year-on-year, increasing the cost of every charging session. (3) The national minimum wage will rise 6.4% from $12.40 to $13.19 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across the energy sector.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for VWC of funding the $720,000 charging hub through a share issue rather than the $450,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Share capital requires no interest or repayment, keeping cash to run 60,000 charging sessions a year. The base rate has moved from 4.9% to 5.65%, so the $450,000 five-year bank loan is getting dearer, while the $270,000 share issue has no finance charge. Each session earns $8.40 ($15.60 − $7.20), or $504,000 at current volume, and that cash can absorb the 15.2% wholesale electricity rise without raising the $15.60 price to fleet drivers.

Point 2: Equity is permanent funding for long-life charging hardware and solar canopies, so no lender can repossess the hubs if the 6.4% charger fault rate delays the expected usage. Investors share the risk of the $720,000 network with the founder, and Sofia Alvarez keeps the bank's credit line free for later hub sites. The cost is some dilution of control, but it is preferable to tying the whole programme to a variable-rate loan in a rising-rate environment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Voltway Charging (VWC), its hub investment and its cost structure.

questions.question_text: Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or direct partnerships with fleet operators. Which should VWC choose to promote its guaranteed charger availability? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: Television could build public awareness of electric charging and show VWC's solar canopies, but airtime is very costly for a 32-person company funding a $720,000 network. Most viewers do not manage fleets, so the campaign would miss the 280 fleet managers described in the survey.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper and can cover one city, yet fleet operators buy charging across several depots and choose networks on reliability, not local jingles. The reach is too small to fill the 60,000 sessions needed against $252,000 of fixed costs, and it does nothing to tackle the 29 billing complaints.

Direct partnerships with fleet operators: Agreements with fleet managers put VWC in front of the exact buyers who value guaranteed charger availability, matching the 73% who would pay $0.45 more and the 61% who choose on reliability. Partnerships can include guaranteed slots and consolidated billing, addressing the complaint problem, and cost far less than television. They take longer to negotiate than a radio campaign and depend on VWC keeping 94.2% availability.

Recommendation: VWC should choose direct partnerships with fleet operators. They reach the surveyed decision-makers, support the $0.45 premium and fit the democratic consultation style. National television is rejected as expensive and untargeted for a business with a $450,000 loan; local radio is rejected as too narrow. VWC should fix the 6.4% fault rate before signing service guarantees. VWC can measure lead quality against the 280-manager survey before renewing the campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to VWC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VWC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of VWC with a justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for VWC of using democratic leadership to reduce its 6.4% charger fault rate and billing complaints.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership asks the 32 technicians and billing staff for ideas on why 6.4% of sessions end in a fault, giving Sofia Alvarez practical information from the people who service the chargers. Consultation builds ownership, so staff are more likely to report small faults early, lifting availability from 94.2% toward the 98% target and protecting the $15.60 price and the $8.40 contribution on every session.

Point 2: Inviting fleet drivers' feedback through the technicians helps trace the 29 billing complaints to their cause, which a top-down instruction might miss. Better involvement raises motivation and retention, reducing reliance on the $1,250 high-voltage certification course for replacements, while keeping the 60,000-session plan on track for the $720,000 hub network. Sofia still takes the final decision, so consultation does not delay urgent repairs. The 14% rise in sessions recorded in Appendix 1 makes that local knowledge valuable as the hubs get busier.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual analysis linked to VWC's faults, complaints and session volume.

questions.question_text: Consider on-the-job coaching for the ten technicians or funded high-voltage certification at $1,250 each. Which should VWC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job coaching: Coaching at the charging hubs is directly relevant to VWC's own rapid chargers, costs no course fee and keeps technicians working on the 60,000-session plan. It suits democratic leadership because experienced staff can share practical fixes for the 6.4% fault rate. Its weakness is that it spreads current habits and gives no recognised certificate, which may matter when fleet managers check competence.

Funded certification: The $1,250 course gives the ten technicians formal high-voltage certification, directly closing the stated skills gap and supporting the reliability message to the 61% of fleet managers who choose networks on reliability. Ten places cost $12,500 (10 × $1,250), a defined sum within the $720,000 programme. The drawback is time away from the hubs, which could lower 94.2% availability and worsen the 29 billing complaints during the course.

Decision: VWC should fund the high-voltage certification, followed by short on-site coaching. Certification addresses the skills gap behind the 6.4% fault rate and strengthens the guarantee that 73% of surveyed managers would pay for, with a known cost of $12,500. On-the-job coaching alone is rejected because it preserves existing habits and provides no credential; VWC can schedule certification in rotations so only a few technicians are away at once. A further consideration is the 14% rise in sessions: as the network grows, informal coaching by a few experts will not scale, so formal certification is the better foundation. VWC should stagger the $1,250 courses to protect the 94.2% availability promised to fleet managers and then measure the 6.4% fault rate before deciding on further places.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to VWC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of VWC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and uses the insert figures.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VWC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $252,000 ÷ ($15.60 − $7.20) = $252,000 ÷ $8.40 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 charging sessions a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.60 − $7.20 = $8.40. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.40.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VWC's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 30,000-session break-even with 60,000 sessions delivered: the margin of safety is 30,000 sessions, a large buffer while 6.4% of sessions fault.
2. Use the $8.40 contribution to test the $0.45 availability premium: the $15.60 price can be modelled with the $7.20 variable cost fixed before fleet managers are offered a discount.
3. Check that 60,000 × $8.40 = $504,000 of contribution covers $252,000 of fixed costs and can service the $450,000 loan as the base rate reaches 5.65%.
4. Benchmark average total cost of $11.40 a session ($252,000 ÷ 60,000 + $7.20) to judge whether charger faults and billing complaints are wasting hub capacity.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.40 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 30,000-session margin of safety despite 6.4% faults; $0.45 premium modelling on $15.60 and $7.20; $504,000 contribution to cover $252,000 fixed costs and the $450,000 loan; unit-cost benchmarking at $11.40 against faults and complaints.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VWC's profitability between 2024 and 2025. Has profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: The surplus after direct costs was $720,000 − $432,000 = $288,000 in 2024 and $840,000 − $462,000 = $378,000 in 2025. Operating return on sales used $72,000 ÷ $720,000 × 100 and $100,800 ÷ $840,000 × 100. Operating return on the capital base used $72,000 ÷ $480,000 × 100 and $100,800 ÷ $560,000 × 100. Revenue rose $120,000 while direct costs rose only $30,000.

Evaluation: Each measure improved. The surplus share of sales rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, which is consistent with the 60,000 sessions spreading network costs despite 6.4% faults. The operating share of sales rose from 10.0% to 12.0%, showing overheads grew more slowly than revenue. Return on capital rose from 15.0% to 18.0% although capital employed increased from $480,000 to $560,000, so the new hubs are generating better returns. Interest payable fell from $12,000 to $10,500, helping the result, yet the 5.65% base rate may reverse that benefit.

Conclusion: VWC's profitability has improved. The 40.0% to 45.0% surplus margin, 10.0% to 12.0% operating margin and 15.0% to 18.0% return on capital all support this. The strongest evidence is the rise in return on capital, because it shows the additional capital in the $720,000 hub network is earning more, not merely that sales are higher. The 15.2% electricity rise is a future risk rather than a 2025 result, so it does not alter this conclusion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements and a justified improved judgement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VWC of offering guaranteed charger availability at $0.45 more per session.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 280 fleet managers found 73% would pay $0.45 more per session for guaranteed availability, and 61% choose networks on reliability. Adding the premium to the $15.60 price with the $7.20 variable cost unchanged raises contribution from $8.40 toward $8.85, giving more cash for the $720,000 hub programme and answering the 29 billing complaints with a clearer service promise.

Disadvantage: A guarantee is costly to honour while 6.4% of sessions end in a fault and availability is 94.2% against a 98% target. Every failed guarantee could lose a fleet contract, and the insert gives no compensation figures, so the net benefit cannot be quantified. With 15.2% wholesale electricity inflation also pushing up the $7.20 cost, the $0.45 premium may not cover the extra expense of keeping spare chargers ready. VWC should check that the 29 billing complaints are falling before extending the guarantee.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to VWC's survey, reliability data and cost structure.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.65%, the 15.2% rise in wholesale electricity prices and the 6.4% minimum wage rise to $13.19 will affect VWC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise (4.9% to 5.65%): The rise is 0.75 percentage points. If the $450,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.0075 × $450,000 = $3,375, a small sum beside $252,000 of fixed costs and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Sofia Alvarez can reduce the risk by fixing the rate, leaving only the higher cost of future borrowing for the $720,000 hub expansion.

Wholesale electricity prices (up 15.2%): This applies to every charging session. The insert gives a single $7.20 variable cost without decomposition, so only an upper bound is defensible: if the whole $7.20 rose 15.2%, that adds 0.152 × $7.20 = $1.09 a session, or about $65,664 a year (60,000 × $1.09), cutting contribution from $8.40 toward $7.31. The $0.45 availability premium supported by 73% of surveyed managers can recover only part of that.

Minimum wage rise (6.4%, $12.40 to $13.19 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or technician pay, so no annual wage total can be invented. The defensible benchmark is productivity: 60,000 sessions ÷ 32 technicians = 1,875 sessions per technician, so the rise is affordable only if that rate holds or the 6.4% fault rate falls.

Conclusion: The 15.2% electricity-price rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds over all 60,000 sessions and directly erodes the $8.40 contribution that funds the hubs, far larger than the conditional $3,375 interest effect, while the wage rise cannot be quantified from the insert. VWC should seek a fixed-energy tariff and lean on the $0.45 premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to VWC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VWC's costs, contribution or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes using derivations shown from insert figures, with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the other two.
